prompt: A plan shows `-/+ resource "aws_instance" "web"`. What will happen to the instance?
hint: Read the two symbols in the order they are written.

choices.text: Its arguments change and it keeps its id
choices.why: That is `~`, update in place. `-/+` gives it a new id.

choices.text: It is destroyed, then a new one is created
choices.why: Yes: destroy and then create replacement, the default order.

choices.text: A new one is created, then the old one is destroyed
choices.why: That order is `+/-`, which needs `create_before_destroy`.

choices.text: It is removed from the state and left running in AWS
choices.why: That is what a `removed` block with `destroy = false` does; the plan shows it with a dot.

prompt: Ana changed only the subnet's `cidr_block`, yet the plan also replaces `aws_instance.web`. Why?
hint: Look at which argument carries `# forces replacement` on the instance.

choices.text: Terraform replaces everything in a configuration when one resource is replaced
choices.why: The VPC was not touched; only what references the subnet followed it.

choices.text: The instance's private address is computed from the range
choices.why: It is, but that is not what the plan blames: the comment is on `subnet_id`.

choices.text: Its `subnet_id` becomes a new, unknown id
choices.why: Right. The new subnet's id is known after apply, and an instance cannot move subnets in place.

choices.text: Tags on the subnet are copied to the instance
choices.why: Nothing copies tags between them; the subnet's tags were not even part of this change.

prompt: In the lesson's plan for the new subnet range, how many resources does the summary line say will be destroyed?
hint: Count the replacements: each one destroys one object.

prompt: During an apply with `create_before_destroy`, Terraform prints `aws_instance.web (deposed object …): Destroying...`. What is the deposed object?
hint: Which of the two instances still has to go?

choices.text: A copy of the state kept as a backup
choices.why: It is an entry in the state, but for a real object, not a backup of the file.

choices.text: The old instance
choices.why: Yes: the replacement exists already, and the old one is kept aside until it is destroyed.

choices.text: The new instance, if its creation failed
choices.why: If creation fails the old one is simply kept; the deposed object is the one being replaced.

choices.text: An instance AWS stopped for maintenance
choices.why: AWS plays no part; deposed is Terraform's word for the object a replacement displaced.

prompt: A security group with `name = "web"` and `create_before_destroy = true` gets a new description, and the apply fails with `InvalidGroup.Duplicate`. What is the fix the lesson uses?
hint: Two groups have to exist at once, for a moment.

choices.text: Remove `create_before_destroy` so the old group goes first
choices.why: That brings the gap back, and on real AWS a group in use cannot be deleted first anyway.

choices.text: Delete the old group by hand and apply again
choices.why: A manual change outside the file is exactly the drift Terraform exists to prevent.

choices.text: Replace `name` with `name_prefix`
choices.why: Yes: Terraform adds a unique suffix, so old and new can coexist during the swap.

choices.text: Keep the old description so nothing is replaced
choices.why: It avoids this replacement and leaves the next one, for any forcing argument, to fail the same way.

prompt: The `web` security group has `name_prefix` and `create_before_destroy`, and its description changes. Put the apply's steps in order.
hint: `+/-` is read left to right.
items: A group with a new suffixed name is created
The old group is kept as a deposed object

prompt: `terraform destroy` in `~/shop/assets` stops with `Instance cannot be destroyed` for the assets bucket. What happened to the logs bucket, which has no `prevent_destroy`?
hint: Is part of a refused plan applied?

choices.text: It was destroyed, since only the assets bucket is protected
choices.why: The whole plan was refused before anything ran; the lesson's `aws s3 ls` still lists it.

choices.text: Nothing
choices.why: Right: Terraform does not apply part of a plan it rejected.

choices.text: It was emptied but kept
choices.why: Terraform never got as far as touching any bucket.

choices.text: It was removed from the state and left in AWS
choices.why: That is a `removed` block's job; a refused destroy changes nothing.

prompt: The assets bucket has `prevent_destroy = true`. Which of these still delete it? Choose all that apply.
hint: The setting lives in one place.

choices.text: A refactor that deletes its resource block, then `apply`
choices.why: Yes: the protection was in the block, and the plan says the bucket is not in configuration.

choices.text: Renaming the bucket in the file, then `apply`
choices.why: The rename forces a replacement, and the plan is refused.

choices.text: Somebody deleting it with the AWS CLI
choices.why: Yes: the setting is Terraform's and reaches nothing outside it.

choices.text: `terraform destroy` with the block unchanged
choices.why: That is the case it refuses, as the lesson showed.

prompt: Why does the lesson value `prevent_destroy` most on the rename of the bucket?
hint: What would a reviewer see in the diff?

choices.text: Renames are the commonest change to buckets
choices.why: The lesson makes no claim about frequency.

choices.text: A rename is slow and blocks the apply for minutes
choices.why: Speed has nothing to do with it; nothing was even attempted.

choices.text: The diff looks like a one-string edit while the plan is a replacement
choices.why: Yes: it catches a destructive change that reads as harmless.

choices.text: AWS forbids renaming buckets that hold objects
choices.why: No bucket can be renamed in place at all; that is why it is a replacement.

prompt: Why does Ana write `ignore_changes = [tags["CostCenter"]]` rather than `ignore_changes = [tags]`?
hint: Who should still own the `Name` tag?

choices.text: `[tags]` is not valid syntax
choices.why: It is valid, and it would have silenced the plan too.

choices.text: So that her own edits to the other tags are still applied
choices.why: Yes: ignoring all tags would make her own future changes look applied and not be.

choices.text: Because the cost tool only runs on weekdays
choices.why: Its schedule plays no part in what Terraform compares.

choices.text: To keep `tags_all` out of the state
choices.why: Both stay in the state; ignore_changes only stops the comparison.

prompt: Inside a `lifecycle` block, the argument that lists attributes Terraform stops comparing with the file once the resource exists is `___`.
hint: Two words joined by an underscore.

prompt: A colleague raised the instance type by hand last week because the configuration's was too small, and proposes `ignore_changes = [instance_type]` to silence the plan. What does the lesson say?
hint: Does another system own this value on purpose?

choices.text: Fine, since the plan noise is the real damage
choices.why: The noise matters, but here the cure is to settle the value, not to hide it.

choices.text: Use `ignore_changes = all` instead, to be safe
choices.why: That stops Terraform looking at the instance at all, the opposite of safe.

choices.text: Put the type in the file, or put the old one back
choices.why: Yes: it is drift with a permission slip, not a value another system owns.

choices.text: Fine, if the colleague also adds a tag explaining it
choices.why: A tag does not change who owns the value; the file and the instance would still disagree, silently.

prompt: Both `terraform apply -replace=aws_instance.web` and `terraform taint aws_instance.web` lead to a replacement. What is the difference the lesson stresses?
hint: Where does each one write the instruction?

choices.text: `-replace` works only with `create_before_destroy`
choices.why: It works on any resource; the `+/-` in the lesson came from the lifecycle setting.

choices.text: `taint` marks the shared state, so a colleague's next plan carries it
choices.why: Right; `-replace` lives in one command and shows in the reviewed plan.

choices.text: `taint` replaces at once, with no plan
choices.why: It only marks; the replacement comes from a later plan and apply.

choices.text: Nothing; they are two names for one command
choices.why: The plans even word it differently: `as requested` against `is tainted`.

prompt: Without a trigger, the plan for release `2026.10.2` updates `user_data` in place. Why does Ana not accept that?
hint: When does a machine read its user data?

choices.text: The running machine would keep the old release
choices.why: Yes: user data runs at first boot, so the new text would sit unused.

choices.text: An in-place update of `user_data` is refused by the AWS API
choices.why: The provider plans it in place because the API allows it.

choices.text: Updating in place would delete the instance's disk without warning
choices.why: An in-place update keeps the instance and its disk; that is the problem here, not the cure.

choices.text: The variable `release` is not allowed inside `user_data`
choices.why: It is allowed, and the plan showed it interpolated.

prompt: Match each comment from a plan in this lesson to what caused it.
hint: Four causes; one option is left over.

pairs.right: a mark written into the state

pairs.left: `will be replaced due to changes in replace_triggered_by`
pairs.right: a change to another resource it names
an argument that cannot be updated in place

right_distractors: a tag added by the cost tool

prompt: In `~/shop/boot`, why does `terraform graph` show no edge from the instance to the object?
hint: How does the instance name the bucket?

choices.text: Instances cannot depend on S3 resources
choices.why: They can, and the reference version gave it exactly that edge.

choices.text: The graph only shows edges between resources of the same service
choices.why: The edges come from references, whatever the service.

choices.text: The bucket is named inside a plain string
choices.why: Yes: to Terraform `s3://shop-boot-dev/boot.sh` is text, not a reference.

choices.text: The object was not created yet
choices.why: The graph comes from the configuration, before and after any apply alike.

prompt: Which change does the lesson prefer for the boot script's hidden dependency?
hint: Is there something the instance could reference?

choices.text: `depends_on = [aws_s3_object.script]` with a comment
choices.why: It works, and it is the second choice: the reason stays outside the expression.

choices.text: Writing the bucket and key into `user_data` through references
choices.why: Yes: the same edge, the name written once, and no `depends_on`.

choices.text: Running `terraform apply` twice
choices.why: The first boot would still race the upload on the first apply.

choices.text: `-parallelism=1` on every apply
choices.why: That serialises everything and still does not say which order is needed.

prompt: Which costs of `depends_on` does the lesson name? Choose all that apply.
hint: Think of the reader, the apply, and data sources.

choices.text: It says to wait but not why
choices.why: Yes; hence the comment beside it.

choices.text: A long list turns a parallel apply into a queue
choices.why: Yes; everything listed has to finish first.

choices.text: It forces the resource to be replaced on every apply
choices.why: That would be a trigger; `depends_on` only orders.

choices.text: On a data source it can push the read to apply time
choices.why: Yes, when the dependency has changes pending.

choices.text: It stores the dependency in the AWS account
choices.why: The edge lives in Terraform's graph only; AWS never hears of it.

prompt: Ana deletes the logs bucket's resource block and runs `terraform plan`. What does the plan propose?
hint: In the state and missing from the file.

choices.text: To destroy the bucket
choices.why: Yes: `because aws_s3_bucket.logs is not in configuration`.

choices.text: To forget the bucket and leave it in AWS
choices.why: That needs a `removed` block with `destroy = false`.

choices.text: No changes, since the file no longer mentions it
choices.why: The state still does, and Terraform reads absence from the file as a wish to destroy.

choices.text: An error asking for `terraform state rm`
choices.why: No error; the plan simply destroys it.

prompt: Why does the lesson prefer a `removed` block to `terraform state rm` for handing the logs bucket to the data team?
hint: The same argument as `-replace` against `taint`.

choices.text: `state rm` deletes the bucket in AWS
choices.why: It only edits the state, like the block; the difference is how the change is made.

choices.text: Terraform 1.7 removed `state rm`
choices.why: 1.7 added the block; the command still exists and lesson 7 uses it.

choices.text: The block is reviewed in a pull request and shows in the plan
choices.why: Yes: the command runs on the shared state and nobody reviews it.

choices.text: Only the block keeps the bucket's objects
choices.why: Neither touches the bucket or its objects.

prompt: After applying the `removed` block, what does each side hold?
hint: Compare `terraform state list` with `aws s3 ls`.

choices.text: The state has both buckets and AWS has only the assets bucket
choices.why: The reverse: the state forgot the logs bucket, AWS kept it.

choices.text: The state has the assets bucket; AWS has both
choices.why: Yes: one entry left the state and nothing in the cloud changed.

choices.text: Both have only the assets bucket
choices.why: That would be a destroy; `destroy = false` kept the bucket.

choices.text: Both still have both, until the block is deleted from the file
choices.why: The apply already took it out of the state; deleting the block later changes nothing.

prompt: A database resource has a fixed `identifier = "shop"` and `create_before_destroy = true`. A change forces a replacement. What should Ana expect, going by this lesson?
hint: It is the security group's story with another resource.

choices.text: A smooth swap, since creating first is always safe
choices.why: Creating first needs both to exist at once, and a fixed unique name forbids it.

choices.text: A collision on the name, with the old one untouched
choices.why: Yes: the creation fails first, and destroying the old one was the next step.

choices.text: The old database destroyed and no new one created
choices.why: With create_before_destroy the destroy comes after a successful create.

choices.text: Terraform renames the old database automatically
choices.why: Terraform never renames to make room; that is what `name_prefix`-style arguments are for.

prompt: A pull request moves every bucket from `main.tf` into a new `storage.tf`, and the assets bucket's block was lost in the move. The bucket has `prevent_destroy`. What does the next plan do?
hint: Where was the protection written?

choices.text: Refuses, because the state remembers `prevent_destroy`
choices.why: The setting is read from the block, and the block is gone.

choices.text: Plans to destroy the bucket
choices.why: Yes, as the lesson's plan showed with the block deleted.

choices.text: Fails because `storage.tf` is not a recognised file name
choices.why: Every `.tf` file in the directory is part of the configuration.

choices.text: Shows no changes, since the other buckets are unchanged
choices.why: The lost bucket is still in the state, so its absence is a change.

hint: One tool is left over.

prompt: Ana reviews a plan whose summary is `2 to add, 0 to change, 2 to destroy`, for a pull request that only edited a subnet. Which conclusions are justified? Choose all that apply.
hint: Replacements are counted as one add and one destroy.

choices.text: Two resources are being replaced
choices.why: Yes, most likely the subnet and something that references it.

choices.text: Nothing will be lost, because the subnet is empty
choices.why: The second replacement may be an instance with a disk; read whose `# forces replacement` it is.

choices.text: The `# forces replacement` comments say which argument caused each
choices.why: Yes; that is the line to read first.

choices.text: The pull request must have edited two files
choices.why: One edited line was enough in the lesson; the second replacement followed a reference.
